chunks.title: Project-Apex README: Project Apex DB
chunks.text: An open-source database for AI agent memory, written in Rust. It writes every change to a write-ahead log, keeps each tenant's records separate, and applies a retried write once. It runs as an embedded library inside your own process. > **Early development. Not ready for production.** There are no search benchmarks yet, so this project makes no speed claims and no comparison with other databases. See [Status](#status) for what is done and what is not.

chunks.title: Project-Apex README: Why
chunks.text: An agent that runs for days has to remember earlier work, keep one user's data apart from another's, and cope with a request that may or may not have been applied. Most projects write that logic themselves, across a vector index, metadata tables, retry code and custom persistence. Project Apex puts the log, tenant scoping and retry handling in the database, to find out whether that is simpler than doing it in application code.

chunks.title: Project-Apex README: What it does
chunks.text: | Feature | How it works | |---|---| | **Durable writes** | Each record is appended to a write-ahead log with a CRC32 checksum. On startup the log is replayed to rebuild state. If the log is corrupt, opening fails with `WAL_CORRUPT` instead of skipping records. | | **Tenant isolation** | Each query runs in a scope: the caller's permissions intersected with the key's allowed scopes. Tests check that a query never returns another tenant's records, including when an index panics. | | **Idempotent writes** | A retried write with the same operation id and identical bytes takes effect once. If the outcome of a commit cannot be determined, the caller gets `OUTCOME_UNKNOWN` instead of a guess. | | **Swappable index** | Search goes through the `AnnIndex` trait. The brute-force `FlatIndex` returns exact results and is the reference any approximate index has to match. No approximate index is wired in yet. |

chunks.title: Project-Apex README: Design
chunks.text: 1. **The log comes first.** The write-ahead log is the source of truth. The index is rebuilt from it on startup and is never trusted from disk. 2. **Isolation has its own tests.** Tenant boundaries are covered by tests for concurrent tenants, a panicking index and replay after a crash. 3. **Numbers come with conditions.** Latency, recall, throughput and memory are reported together, with the dataset, hardware and build settings used. 4. **Evidence is tied to a snapshot.** Each test result is recorded against a digest of the source. Change a file and the old result no longer counts until it is re-run.

chunks.title: Project-Apex README: Repository layout
chunks.text: The crates keep their internal `atlas-*` names. The public name is Project Apex DB.

chunks.title: CausalMesh README: CausalMesh
chunks.text: [](LICENSE) [](pyproject.toml) **A research-grade experimental platform for separating _information_ from _enforcement_ in distributed LLM coding agents.** ---

chunks.title: CausalMesh README: Install
chunks.text: Put the gate in front of your own agent's tools: A refused call never reaches the handler, and the refusal is signed evidence that `causalmesh verify` checks offline. The full local journey, with no key and no model, is [`examples/cli_demo/`](examples/cli_demo/README.md). The experiment harness (four arms, the task suite, `experiment run`) is not in the wheel: `git clone` the repository for it. **Pre-alpha.** Every run so far used a deterministic mock agent; nothing here has been run against a hosted model, so nothing here says how real coding agents behave. See [`docs/backlog.md`](docs/backlog.md). ---

chunks.title: CausalMesh README: The research question
chunks.text: > How much of the coordination benefit in distributed LLM coding agents comes from **information**, and how much comes from **enforcement**? When multiple coding agents work on a shared codebase, they interfere: they make stale reads, duplicate each other's work, and overwrite each other's changes. Systems that fix this usually do two things at once — they *tell* agents what peers are doing, and they *prevent* agents from conflicting. Because these arrive together, their individual contributions are unknown. CausalMesh separates them experimentally. The contribution is **measurement**, not the invention of a new coordination mechanism.

chunks.title: CausalMesh README: Experimental design
chunks.text: Four arms, manipulating exactly two factors: | Arm | Information | Enforcement | Description | |:---:|---|---|---| | **C0** | none | none | Fully isolated agents, no peer visibility | | **C1** | unbounded transcript | none | Agents see a full conversational transcript | | **C2** | bounded structured metadata | none | Agents see typed events describing what changed | | **C3** | bounded structured metadata | write claims | Metadata **plus** enforced exclusive write claims | The contrasts that answer the question: Everything other than information and enforcement is held constant: task, model, decoding parameters, agent roles, repository fixture, tool semantics, success criteria, randomization protocol. Anything that cannot be held constant is recorded and treated as a potential confound.

chunks.title: CausalMesh README: Architecture
chunks.text: Dependencies run one way only. Analysis never mutates runtime state, the verifier never depends on the relay being online, and the observer is strictly read-only.

chunks.title: Auralis README:
chunks.text: Push-to-talk dictation for Windows. Hold **Ctrl+Space**, speak, release — cleaned-up transcribed text is inserted into whatever application currently has focus. Or tap **Ctrl+Shift+Space** for hands-free continuous dictation. Auralis runs entirely on-device: no cloud STT, no cloud LLM cleanup, no telemetry.

chunks.title: Auralis README: How it works
chunks.text: - **Mic capture** — [cpal](https://github.com/RustAudio/cpal), default input device - **VAD** — [webrtc-vad](https://github.com/valenzuela/webrtc-vad) trims leading/trailing silence - **Denoise** — RNNoise via [nnnoiseless](https://github.com/jneem/nnnoiseless) (pure Rust) - **STT** — [whisper.cpp](https://github.com/ggerganov/whisper.cpp) via [whisper-rs](https://github.com/tazz4843/whisper-rs), quantized GGUF weights, beam search with temperature fallback, optional CUDA acceleration - **Text cleanup** — local rules only: capitalization, terminal punctuation, disfluency removal, and a spoken-correction heuristic ("actually, change X to Y") - **Insertion** — simulated keystrokes via [enigo](https://github.com/enigo-rs/enigo), with a clipboard fallback. A spoken correction backspaces the text Auralis just typed and replaces it in place

chunks.title: Auralis README: Text cleanup modes
chunks.text: How much the text layer is allowed to rewrite what you said is a setting (tray **Settings → Text cleanup**). `raw` always stays available, so the transcript can be inspected without any rules in the way: | mode | disfluencies removed | capitalized | terminal punctuation | |---|---|---|---| | `raw` | no | no | no | | `clean` *(default)* | no | yes | yes | | `polished` | yes | yes | yes | | `developer` | yes | no | no | `developer` exists because dictating `cargo test --locked` into a terminal should not acquire a trailing period. Disfluency removal is deliberately conservative — only tokens that are not also ordinary English words, so "summary" and "ahead" survive while a standalone "um" does not.

chunks.title: Auralis README: Audio quality analysis
chunks.text: Every utterance is measured before VAD trimming and denoising, and reported at `debug` level (`RUST_LOG=auralis_runtime=debug`): speech-to-noise ratio in dB, the fraction of frames the VAD called speech, RMS level, and whether the input clipped — clipping also warns, since it is the most common fixable cause of bad transcripts. SNR reads `n/a` rather than a fabricated number when the buffer has no speech frames or no noise frames to compare against.

chunks.title: Auralis README: Accuracy knobs
chunks.text: The single biggest lever is model size. `base.en` (~59 MB) is the fast default; `small.en` (~190 MB) is noticeably better on proper nouns and accented speech at roughly 3x the decode cost: The installer bundles **Whisper base.en** (OpenAI, MIT licence; see `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`) so dictation works offline on first launch. It is a third-party model used as an interim default, not an Auralis model, and it is not part of any Auralis model release. Auralis never downloads models: add more ggml `.bin` files to the per-user app data `models` folder (the repo's `models/` folder is also searched in dev builds). Any model there appears in the **Active model** picker. Decoding uses beam search (width 5) with whisper.cpp's temperature-fallback thresholds and `no_context`, which together suppress the repetition loops that greedy decoding with cross-utterance context is prone to. This is the Phase 1 vertical slice described in [`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-01-phase1-vertical-slice-design.md`](docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-01-phase1-vertical-slice-design.md): a real, daily-usable dictation

chunks.title: Archi.dev README: # Archi.dev
chunks.text: Archi.dev is a visual backend architecture studio for designing APIs, workflows, infrastructure, and agent-oriented execution graphs before writing code. It combines a multi-tab canvas, deterministic graph models, architecture validation, optional AI-assisted graph generation, OpenAPI export, and runtime simulation in a single Next.js application.

chunks.title: Archi.dev README: Overview
chunks.text: Archi.dev is built around a simple idea: backend systems should be modeled explicitly. Instead of burying architecture inside scattered source files, the studio lets you define: - APIs and contracts - background and synchronous processes - database and infrastructure capabilities - service boundaries - agent execution plans and graph patches The visual workspace is backed by structured graph data, not opaque editor state.

chunks.title: Archi.dev README: Multi-tab backend workspace
chunks.text: The studio is split into focused tabs: - `api` - `database` - `functions` - `agent` Each tab has its own graph while still participating in a shared system model.

chunks.title: Archi.dev README: Canvas-based architecture modeling
chunks.text: You can compose systems using React Flow nodes for: - API bindings - processes and workflows - databases and queues - infrastructure blocks - service boundaries - API endpoint references

chunks.title: Archi.dev README: Passive architecture validation
chunks.text: The app continuously validates the workspace and surfaces: - node-level validation badges - architecture warnings and errors - generation-readiness checks before code export

chunks.title: shortlist-ai README: AI Resume Screener & Skill Gap Analyzer 🚀
chunks.text: A production-ready, serverless ATS intelligence platform built with Next.js, Vercel, and AWS (Free Tier). Designed for recruiters and hiring managers to instantly analyze skill gaps and shortlist probabilities.

chunks.title: shortlist-ai README: 🏗 Architecture
chunks.text: The system is built on a **Serverless Event-Driven Architecture** designed for high availability and low latency.

chunks.title: shortlist-ai README: High-Level Data Flow
chunks.text: 1. **Ingestion Layer**: * The user uploads a resume (PDF/DOCX) via the frontend. * This triggers a request to `/api/upload` which securely stores the raw file in **Amazon S3**. * Simultaneously, the file is processed by the **Parser Engine** (using `mammoth` and `pdf2json`) to extract raw text. 2. **Analysis Layer**: * The extracted text and the provided Job Description are sent to the `/api/analyze` endpoint. * **Skill Intelligence Engine**: This core logic calculates the match score using: * **TF-IDF & Cosine Similarity**: For semantic relevance. * **Regex Taxonomy Matching**: To identify specific hard skills. * **Heuristic Scoring**: To determine a final "match percentage". 3. **Persistence Layer**: * The structured analysis results (scores, matched skills, missing skills) are saved to **Amazon DynamoDB** for fast retrieval. * Recruiters can query these results instantly via the `/history` view.

chunks.title: shortlist-ai README: 🛠 Tech Stack
chunks.text: - **Frontend**: Next.js 15 (App Router), Vanilla CSS (Custom Design System), Lucide Icons - **Backend**: Next.js Serverless API Routes (Node.js runtime) - **Infrastructure**: Vercel (Compute), AWS S3 (Storage), AWS DynamoDB (Database) - **ML/NLP**: `natural` (Tokenization), `compute-cosine-similarity`, Regex-based Entity Extraction

chunks.title: shortlist-ai README: ✨ Features
chunks.text: - **Resume Parsing**: Robust extraction from PDF & DOCX. - **Skill Gap Analysis**: Identifies missing, present, and extra skills based on JD. - **Match Scoring**: Multi-factor scoring algorithm (Semantic + Keyword + Skill Match). - **Recruiter Probability**: "Probability of Shortlisting" score modeled on heuristic hiring patterns. - **Serverless & Fast**: No cold-start heavy ML models; extremely fast, deterministic execution.
